justification_text:
The point estimates for each time horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—are driven by the expectation of how the variable of interest will evolve over time based on current conditions and recent trends. For example, the 1-day forecast (109.2) assumes very little time for meaningful changes to occur, so it is closely tied to the most recent observed value or short-term patterns. The 1-week estimate (108.8) reflects slightly more uncertainty, as there is more time for fluctuations, but it still leans heavily on visible trends and immediate market dynamics. For the 1-month estimate (107.5), the assumption is that over a longer horizon, mean-reverting tendencies or broader influences (such as economic fundamentals) may cause the value to shift more perceptibly from recent levels.

The confidence intervals widen as the forecast horizon increases because uncertainty grows the further out we project. For the 1-day forecast, the range between the lower and upper bounds of the 90% confidence interval (108.0 to 110.5) is narrow, reflecting limited opportunity for major changes in such a short time. Over 1 week or 1 month, though, more uncertainty is introduced by possible shifts in external factors, random fluctuations, and even structural changes. The wider intervals account for these cumulative uncertainties, whether they come from volatility in the system itself or new information that could impact the variable unexpectedly.

Risks or events that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include rare but impactful shocks, such as geopolitical events, major policy announcements, or unexpected disruptions in supply chains or markets. These types of events are difficult to predict and are not fully captured by standard probabilistic models, which tend to focus on historically observed patterns. Additionally, if the underlying system is undergoing a transition or a structural break—such as a change in dynamics due to new policies or shifts in demand—our models may understate the likelihood of outcomes falling outside predicted ranges. These possibilities, while unlikely in most cases, highlight why no forecast can account for all potential scenarios with perfect precision.
